qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

Directive (EU) 2023/1791, Article 16(2), stipulates that meters and heat cost allocators already installed but which are not remotely readable must be rendered remotely readable or replaced by 1 January 2027, unless a Member State demonstrates that this is not cost-efficient. In blocks of flats, this may mean replacing devices that are still in working order before the end of their operational life, with the costs potentially being passed on to flat owners and occupants. In light of the foregoing: 1.
What criteria, in the Commission’s view, should Member States apply when assessing the cost-efficiency of introducing remote meter reading for existing meters and heat cost allocators?
In the Commission’s view, does Article 16(2) of the Directive allow the burden of proving that remote meter reading is not cost-efficient to be shifted onto individual flat owners and occupants?

Does the Commission consider that, when assessing cost-efficiency, account should be taken of the total costs of installation, operation, maintenance and replacement of equipment in relation to the energy savings that can realistically be achieved?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.11.2026) To empower final customers to better manage their energy consumption, it is important that they have access to comprehensive information on their own energy use. This information should be available through digital tools, and to make that possible, meters and sub-meters are important, including remotely readable devices. The Energy Efficiency Directive (EED)1 takes into account that in some circumstances it may not be technically possible and cost-efficient to ensure remote metering. The Directive leaves for the Member States to decide on criteria when assessing the cost-efficiency, but requires that the general criteria, methodologies and procedures to determine technical non-feasibility and non-cost-effectiveness has to be clearly set out and published. The deadline of 2027 was intended to give sufficient time and thus minimise the risk of sunk costs arising due to devices having to be replaced significantly before they have been depreciated. The EED does not contain specific provisions regulating whether the burden of proving that remote meter reading is not cost-efficient could be shifted onto individual flat owners and occupants. Member States shall assess cost-efficiency based on the conditions set out in the Directive, Article 15(1) and recital 94 of the EED, and the guidelines provided by the Commission for the implementation of the relevant provision (Commission Recommendation (EU) 2019/16602). The EED does not require a specific technology, as clarified in Recital (97) of the EED. Finally, the EED does not contain specific provisions regulating if flat owners and occupants may use a less costly solution that meets the requirements of the Directive, where several technically suitable solutions exist.
